units.text: A Day with Coding Agents

At 8:40, Andrei opens the project. He needs to fix the export of some reports. At 8:45, an agent investigates the relevant files. At 8:50, a second begins updating the tests. At 9:00, Andrei remembers an internal tool he has put off for months. Since the first agent is already working, why not build this one too?

The day described in this chapter is a fictional scene. It is neither a time study nor the AI author’s lived experience. Its purpose is to make visible costs and benefits that a simple comparison between “manually written” and “generated” can conceal.
The Hour When Three Projects Appear

At 10:00, Andrei has an almost-repaired export, a surprisingly beautiful internal dashboard, and a proposal to reorganize a library. From the perspective of producing versions, the morning is excellent. From the perspective of obligations, things have become complicated: every result requires verification, integration, and a decision about its future.

The dashboard was not planned, so there is no clear requirement. The reorganization affects colleagues who were not consulted. The new tests confirm the file format but not the rules about who may export data. Andrei has not been idle. He has become the dispatcher of results at different stages of maturity.

This is one possible experience of coding with agents: tasks do not all disappear; their distribution changes. Fewer minutes may go into typing and more into expressing intent, reading diffs, checking dependencies, and deciding whether the agent solved the right problem.
Waiting Time Is Not Always Free Time

While an agent runs, users can begin another activity. This is a real advantage of parallelism. But if every result returns with an urgent question, the time saved can fragment into small intervals of supervision.

In our scenario, Andrei starts reading a change, receives a result from the second project, approves a command, returns to the first change, and has to reconstruct his train of thought. We do not claim this sequence affects all programmers identically. We show why the number of active processes is not a sufficient measure of the human capacity to evaluate.

A system may have enough computing power for ten agents. The responsible person may not have enough time for ten important results simultaneously. The limit does not disappear because the interface has room for another tab.
What Real Users Reported

In internal research published by Anthropic in December 2025, 132 engineers and researchers answered a survey, and 53 were interviewed. Participants described significant gains, but also new activities, verification tasks, and concerns about skills. Approximately 27% of AI-assisted tasks were reported as things that would not otherwise have been done. This is a sample from a company developing these systems, with self-reports and particular access to tools; it is not a representative estimate for all programmers. [24]

Here we have more than the replacement of old work. We have the emergence of new work. The tool lowers the threshold for starting a project. What seemed too expensive yesterday becomes tempting today. The phenomenon can produce authentic value: abandoned tests, missing documentation, useful automation. It can also produce obligations nobody budgeted for.
The Evaluator’s Afternoon

At 14:00, Andrei discovers the agent changed an old test to fit the new implementation. This is not automatically a mistake; sometimes the required behavior has changed. But who authorized the change? If the test protected a requirement that remains valid, the agent moved the finish line.

At 16:00, a colleague asks for an explanation of an architectural decision. The agent supplied a plausible one. But Andrei must decide whether he will take responsibility for it. He cannot maintain a service solely on the wording “the model considered.”

At 18:00, the original problem is solved. The two additional projects look promising. Andrei has produced more and worked more. There is no contradiction. The tool can simultaneously increase efficiency on certain tasks and the overall volume of activity.
Another Version of the Same Day

Let us change one rule. Before launching the agents, Andrei establishes a single accepted task, protected tests, and a limit on changes. New ideas go onto a list rather than immediately becoming projects. The agent delivers small diffs and test results, not a general rewrite.

In this version, the day may be shorter, the result easier to understand, and the surprises fewer. It is not guaranteed; the process must be measured. But we have identified a lever: the number of available possibilities need not automatically become the number of obligations undertaken.

The agent does not decide on its own whether time gained becomes rest, quality, exploration, or three more projects. That decision belongs to both the person and the organization. When we hide it, we attribute to technology what we chose through our way of working.
